For the final exam, all the wizards of each class must assemble at the legendary Ravenskeep… but every last one of them has procrastinated, distracted by learning new spells. They’ve also used all their potions—they can’t show up unprepared, with empty potion bottles! Help your wizards get to Ravenskeep as quickly as possible. Using their magic they could even move the very towers atop which they stand to get there more easily! But how can they refill their potion bottles along the way? Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Goal 3 Playing 4 Movement cards 4.1 Cards that move a wizard 4.2 Cards that move a tower 4.3 Cards that move either 5 Imprisoning Wizards 6 Spells 7 End of game Overview Your main goal is to fill your potion bottles and get all of your wizards into the black Ravenskeep. On your turn you can choose to play up to 2 action cards, which let you move a tower (or an upper subsection of one) or move one of your own wizards. Whenever you cover up a wizard (including your own) with a tower, you fill one of your potion bottles. You must memorise where your covered wizards are so you can free them later! You can also cast an optional spell, which costs a number of filled potions. Maximum potions you'll be able to get is 5, and unused potions are a tie breaker at the end, so use them sparingly. Easy peasy, you place a tower on a wizard to fill your potion. Then use those potions for the effects in the middle. Bottle gone and game moves on. The black Ravenskeep piece doesn't count as a tower. When you move a wizard onto it, the Ravenskeep moves around the board and your turn ends. Everything moves clockwise. When one person has all bottles filled, and all their wizards in the Ravenskeep, the game is over. Goal Fill all of your potion bottles and get all of your wizards into Ravenskeep (it doesn’t matter which you do first). Move your wizards into Ravenskeep with good timing. Fill your potion bottles by moving towers onto wizards to imprison them. But if your own wizards are imprisoned, you must free them so they can get to Ravenskeep! Playing Play goes clockwise, beginning with the starting player. On your turn, you must play 2 cards from your hand face up on the discard pile, one at a time. For each card you play, perform its move if at all possible. Alternatively, you may forgo both actions to discard your entire hand and advance any 1 tower 1 space clockwise (see Cards That Move a Tower, below). In either case, at any time during your turn, you may spend full potion bottles to cast one magic spell (see Casting a Spell). Finally, draw to refill your hand to 3 cards. Each time the deck is depleted, shuffle the discards to form a new deck. Movement cards There are 3 types of movement cards: 1. Cards that move a wizard; these depict a wizard on the right page of the book. 2. Cards that move a tower; these depict a tower on the left page of the book. 3. Cards that can move either a wizard or a tower; these depict a tower on the left, a wizard on the right. Cards that move a wizard Move one of your own visible wizards. If the card depicts a number, advance the wizard clockwise exactly that number of spaces. If the card depicts a die, roll the die to determine exactly how far a wizard will advance. For each additional die depicted on the card, you may reroll the die once; however, if you do, you forfeit the previous roll. Only after your final roll must you choose a wizard to move. Whenever a wizard’s move ends in a space with a tower in it, the wizard goes atop the tower, rather than in the space. Each tower and each empty space can hold up to 6 wizards. [Rating: 1/10] It cost toooooo much for a children game, i paid 40 € for what? A player mat and some cardboard tower?

[Rating: 1/10] I was expecting more from the hype, but this was so..... boring and safe. I'm usually the worst with memory, and even I could still memorize where all the wizards were. So it's a lot of expensive gimmicky components for a simple race. Also fill up potions for spells that are extremely logical, instead of wacky.  Thinking of many games where players alter the racecourse, and they're all better than this. This was probably inspired by Camel Up, but this has even LESS humor, how is that even possible? Or based on Ludo, which has more drama thanks to the dice (why do eurogame designers surgically 

[Rating: 2/10] I could see this being a fun kids' game, but that's about it. The amount of times you find yourself stuck without being able to take a meaningful action is far too high.

[Rating: 2/10] Horribly chaotic to the point where it is a seriously convoluted and unfun game. Probably great fun for those who like zany comebacks and endless BOOYA!-moments, but given that opportunities are mostly unpredictable means that this game cannot really be played to win. I will not willingly play this monstrosity again, and will insist on something wholesome instead, like Drop It! or some equivalent.

[Rating: 2/10] The extreme amount of randomness keeps this from being enjoyable. You get a small hand of cards with movement points on them. You play one to move one of your figures clockwise in the circle. Sometimes you can also move tower pieces along the same circle. If you cover any meeples, they get stuck until they are uncovered. The goal is at the end of the ring at the start of the game, but each time someone gets a meeple into the goal, the goal moves along the same ring. The utter chaos created by all these elements clashing is more than I can enjoy.

[Rating: 2/10] I bounced off Wandering Towers harder than I have anything in a very long time. With more than four players, you have so little control over what's happening, you're just kind of riding the wave (or magically moving tower). We played with 6, and most players weren't even remotely close to meeting their win conditions. It was between two players and first place was still very comfortably in the lead by the time they put us out of our misery.  The game's card draw/action mechanic is infuriating. [Rating: 3/10] :star::star::nostar::nostar::nostar:  Good fun of moving witches and towers around. Covering up other players witches often results in laughs on the table.

[Rating: 3/10] Rated after 1 play. The game looks fantastic and has a greate table presence. The game worked fine until the final turns where I had three turns where I couldn't do anything with my cards. This is frustrating and drags the end unnecessarily.

[Rating: 3/10] I never thought I would say this Kramer and kiesling made a game I did not enjoy This game is all luck and random There's no way to plan ahead and if your wizards get trapped you feel like your next turn is useless

[Rating: 3/10] Played at 5p in Nov 2024, and it's not for me. I don't generally like memory games, and this has a decent component of that as you track where your three people are (so you can't even safely go to the bathroom on other player's turns).   Then I think it's difficult to truly make any sort of strategy since very often, the person before or two turns before you will play a card or two to shift the state of the board too much, rendering your previous plans useless.
